hybrid.answer:
**Out of the box: it depends on the leather.** His videos are about Blundstones, so his advice applies most directly to those.

- **Regular (finished, oiled) leathers:** He read out Blundstone's own FAQ, which says most of its boots come pretreated and that the company does *not* recommend treating them out of the box [1]. That is Blundstone's guidance, which he relays.
- **Distressed leathers** (rustic brown, Crazy Horse brown, rustic black): The FAQ says these don't carry the same pretreatment [2]. Here his own view is firm. - **Keep in mind:** Oil and wax will darken the leather [4][5]. He says boots lighten again with wear, though maybe not all the way back to their original shade [5]. - If they look or feel dry, or water isn't beading on top, add more wax or oil [8].
- Clean them regularly when they're dirty, since dirt wears the leather down faster [8].
- Always work in this order: clean, condition, then wax [9].

In his earlier videos (2019) he gave rougher guides. He said you might have to wax monthly, or weekly if you're really hard on your boots, though you probably won't need to go that far [10]. He also said any leather you haven't conditioned in a few months should get conditioned [11].

He uses Otterwax products in these videos. He has a referral code with them, though he says the restoration video isn't sponsored by Otterwax [12].

**How to do it:** Make sure the boot is clean first [7]. Go in this order: clean, condition, then wax [8]. Use thin coats, since "less is more" [9].

## How often?
His most recent take (2022) is that he treats them "when I feel like they need it" and admits he probably does too little [10]. His cues [11]:

- Looks dry, feels dry, or water isn't beading on top: time for more wax or oil.
- Dirty: clean them, because dirt wears leather down faster.

Earlier rules of thumb he gave in 2019:

- If any leather item hasn't been conditioned in a few months, condition it [12].
- Waxing might mean every month, "maybe every week if you just go super crazy with your boots" [13]. Also brush the salt off in winter [14].

**How it worked out for him:** His rustic Blundstones went a full year untreated after that first oiling [15]. They still kept his feet dry enough for crossing a stream or standing in mud [16]. Wax and oil darken boots, but they lighten again as you wear them [17].

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
**Yes. The Iron Snail says the Levi's 501 Shrink-to-Fit shrinks when it gets wet, mostly in the waist, and then loosens up again as you wear it.** His main advice is to buy them bigger to start with.

**Size up (his most consistent advice)**
- In his 2025 value ranking he still likes the 501 STF and says it'll shrink in the bathtub, so "you should usually go two sizes up" [1].
- In 2021 he admitted it took him four pairs of 501s to accept that Levi's sizing advice is right: two sizes bigger in the waist and two inches longer [2]. If you usually wear a 34, he says get a 36 [3]. Tried on before soaking they'll be too big, "but trust me" [4].
- In his 2023 comparison he went up two sizes, and expected the STFs to end up smaller than a regular rinsed pair of 501s in your normal size [5].

**How you wash them matters**
- In 2023 his shrunk STFs did come out smaller than regular rinsed 501s [6]. He thinks a dryer would have made them "a lot smaller" [7].
- His pair looked better because he didn't use super hot water and didn't machine-dry them. His advice: "don't toss your stfs in the dryer or rinse them that hot" [8].

**What happened with his first pair (2019–2020)**
- He ignored Levi's advice and bought a 29 waist [9]. After a hot soak the waist was very tight, "definitely around the waist" [10], but the length looked "pretty much the same" [11].
- A week later the upper thigh and waist had stretched enough that he could wear a belt [12].
- A year on he said he could barely pull them on at first, but they had become a really good fit [13]. He also said he would have gone a 32 length [14].

**In short:** they'll get tighter after the first soak, especially in the waist, and then stretch with wear. He suggests buying two sizes up in the waist, adding about two inches of length, and skipping very hot water and the dryer.

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
The Iron Snail cuffs mostly for **length and overall look**. He thinks jeans that look too long just look bad. More recently, he feels uncuffed wider-legged pants don't suit his style.

**His most recent take (July 2020):** After a year in his Levi's 501s, he admitted they were actually on the short side. He would have gotten a 32 length. He still cuffs them anyway because he doesn't think his current style lends itself to wider-legged pants worn uncuffed [1].

**Length comes first (June 2019):** When he first tried on the 501 Shrink-to-Fits, he said the basic cuff made them fit and feel a little better. He explained that for him "it's all about length": if jeans look too long, they look bad. He also noted the cuff can't be too thick [2]. He tried a pin roll on the same wide, unshrunk 501s and thought it slimmed them a bit and looked a little better, though they were still wider than he liked [3].

**When he skips the cuff (November 2019):** In his L.L. Bean boot review, he said he "always used to cuff" his jeans. Lately, though, he'd come to like wearing them down over his boots a bit more. He sees this as a slightly older style that calms down loud statement boots like Bean boots [4]. For a more workwear look with those boots, he suggested a 7 to 7.5 inch leg opening pulled down over the boot [5].

So he isn't strictly a cuffer. He cuffs to get the length and silhouette he likes, but with boots like Bean boots he has leaned toward leaving his jeans uncuffed.

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
**Short version:** In his only head-to-head, The Iron Snail sides with **Solovair** unless the yellow stitching matters to you. He calls them cheaper and better built than Made in England Docs [1].

**His Solovair vs. Made in England comparison (April 2022)**
- **Leather and midsoles:** He thinks the Made in England leather is probably on par with Solovair's, and the midsoles are too [2].
- **Shank and comfort:** No Dr. Martens have a shank, Made in England included [3]. Solovairs do, so he finds them more comfortable over long periods [4]. The trade-off is that Solovairs are tougher to break in, but you get more comfort down the line [5].
- **Resoling:** Solovairs are Goodyear welted in a more conventional way, so they're easier to resole [4].
- **Same boot, cheaper:** He says Solovairs come from one of the original makers of Docs [6]. Their derby eight-eye boot is essentially the exact same boot as Docs [7], and they cost less than Made in England Docs [2].
- **The one catch:** Solovair doesn't do the yellow stitching. If that's a big deal to you, he says you have to go Made in England [8].
- **His own pair wasn't perfect:** After eight wears, a back tab ripped off and a bootlace snapped. He assumed it was a manufacturing defect and contacted them [9]. He also noted he wasn't sponsored by either brand [10].

**His later look at Made in England Docs (May 2023)**
He didn't bring Solovair into this video. Instead he compared the $260 Made in England 1460 with the Made in Thailand version, which costs $90 less [11]. The upgrades he lists include:
- a felted midsole instead of foam [12]
- a heavier rubber outsole [13]
- a better ribbed welt [14]
- a slimmer last [15]

His verdict was that, objectively, they're "probably not" worth the extra $90 [16]. He sees them as a buy for mega fans of the brand [17]. That keeps his lean the same: Made in England Docs are mainly worth it if you specifically want the Dr. Martens brand and look, and in 2022 he pointed value-minded buyers to Solovair instead.

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** he hasn't talked about multi-day hikes specifically. His experience suggests Blundstones can handle hiking, but he flags weak ankle support as the main drawback on mountain terrain.

**What he's said about hiking in them:**
- In his one-year review (2020), he wore his pair daily for about eight months and "went on a lot of hikes with them climbed a lot of mountains with them" [1]. His caveat is that they "are not good boots for mountaining apparently because they don't have uh good ankle support." Still, after going up and down a few mountains in Maine, they got scuffed but "held up well" [2].
- He got more scuffs than he expected, though he puts that down to his own clumsiness kicking rocks on the way down [3].

**Water and mud:** In his 2020 pond test, after a year without re-treating them, he concluded you "should be good" if you're "crossing a brook or a stream or you just want to stand in some mud for a little bit" [4]. In his 2019 review he said he wouldn't stand in water for hours, since they're water resistant rather than waterproof [5]. By 2023 he said his pair had "remained probably my most water resistant boots through it all" [6].

**Keep them treated:** He recommends them "100% if you're going to treat them" and stresses that you have to keep them treated to keep that water resistance [7]. If yours are a distressed style like rustic brown, he later pointed to Blundstone's FAQ saying those leathers don't carry the same pretreatment as finished, oiled leather [8]. Conditioning them before a long trip would follow his advice.

**What he hasn't covered:** He hasn't addressed comfort over several consecutive days, carrying a heavy pack, or how they compare with dedicated hiking boots for a trip like yours. So whether they're right for your 4-day hike depends on the terrain. On rocky or mountainous trails, his ankle-support warning is the thing to weigh.

- **Right tool for the job:** his overall view is that they're decent for work but "not anything incredible," a balance of tough and casual rather than purpose-built [9]. **Bottom line:** going by what he's said, Blundstones are fine on trails and in wet conditions, especially if they're broken in and freshly treated. On rough, rocky or steep terrain, or with a heavy pack, his own warning about ankle support is the thing to weigh.

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
**Short version:** The Iron Snail thinks the **1907 is the better buy of the two**. In his 2021 review he calls it "the best Red Wing Moc Toe Boot" [1]. His case is mostly about value: for a little more money you get several extras.

**The differences he points out (2021):**
- **Price:** The 1907s are about $10 more than the 875s [2].
- **Welt:** The 875 is Goodyear welted, which he calls durable and pretty water resistant [3]. The extra space from the welt leaves room for cork that molds to your foot over time [4]. The 1907 adds a storm welt, which he calls "invaluable" [5]. On how Red Wing's storm welt actually works, he passes on the popular view from Reddit that it's basically another strip of leather stitched onto the welt [6]. He adds that he's "not quite sure" [7].
- **Leather footbed:** The 1907 comes with Red Wing's leather footbed, which he says normally costs about $40 on its own [8]. You can pull it out at night to help the boots dry faster [9].
- **Leather laces:** These are included with the 1907 and are normally about $15 [10]. He corrects his own maths: the extras are really worth about $45 once you subtract the extra $10 you paid [11].

**His water test on the 1907:** One boot leaked almost immediately at the welt line, which he found a bit of a letdown [12]. Even so, he has "no doubt" they'd be fine in rain, grass or mud [13].

**What they share and his later views:**
- In 2022 he noted that both boots use crepe soles, which he feels will break down faster than a Vibram sole [14].
- In the same video he called both of them more beefily built, and better if you need a tough boot [15]. Even so, he preferred the Red Wing 3335 over both for everyday hikes and walks [16].
- By 2023 he said the 875s and 1907s each "have their own characteristics" that he really likes [17].

He hasn't directly compared how the two fit or look against each other.

questions.question: Would you recommend this or the flint and tinder for someone who would use it like a rain jacket but also a windbreaker and a spring light jacket?

hybrid.answer:
It isn't clear which jacket "this" refers to. The most common comparison in his videos is the **Barbour** against the **Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker**, so that's what's below. The Iron Snail has never directly picked between them for a rain, wind and spring jacket, but here's what he's said about each for that kind of use.

**Barbour (his most-praised option for weather)**
- In his 2025 ranking he said Barbour won because of its weather coverage, while noting that "for the most part, it's not a designated rain jacket" [1].
- He calls its 6 oz Sylkoil the lightest fabric in that lineup. It has room to layer, so he thinks you can wear it in fall, summer or spring and be comfortable [2].
- For bad weather it has a throat latch, hood snaps and storm cuffs, which he calls "really helpful in inclement weather" [3]. You can also add or remove liners as the temperature changes [4].
- On wind: in his 2021 Barbour guide he explained that the thornproof finish (as opposed to Sylkoil) gives "added wind resistance and added water resistance" because the weave is tighter [5]. If windbreaker use matters most, that is the finish he says performs better.

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker (his easy all-rounder)**
- He says it's "literally built for everyone." It's a lighter weight, comfortable, cut for full movement and goes with anything [6].
- It's lined, so you don't get wax on your skin. Its real selling point for him is the price: $300 for a lined, US-made jacket in Martexin fabric, which makes it "hard to not recommend" [7].
- Note that Huckberry sponsored that 2025 video. He says he'd praised the jacket many times before the sponsorship [8].
- In 2023 he reviewed an unlined Huckberry waxed trucker. He said it can be worn when it's a little warmer and pictured its wearer as someone who wears it "when it's raining outside with a hat" [9].

**Putting it together:** if your priority is foul-weather protection (hood, storm cuffs, throat latch, and thornproof's extra wind resistance if you choose that finish), the Barbour is the one he credits with those features. **Red Wing 3335s (2022 review)**
- He went **true to size** and they "fit fine" [1].
- The catch is the **shape**. He describes a very slim profile, partly because the outsole is very thin, and the boots taper down [1].
- With thin cotton socks in warm weather he had no discomfort. With wool socks his toes felt squished and he couldn't wiggle them much [2].
- In a later video he called them lighter-weight boots that feel more nimble and are easier for walking or a light hike [3].

**The 875s and the moc toe side**
- He has only talked about the 875s in terms of construction, not fit. He calls the 1907s and 875s "more beefily constructed" than the 3335s [4].
- On the 1907s, Red Wing's other moc toe, he wore his usual boot size (an 8) and said they "fit perfect" [5].
- His general advice for Red Wings and most leather boots is to buy them **snug, not squished**, so the stiff leather can mold to your feet over time [5].

**Bottom line:** by his account, you'd go true to size in both. If you wear thick wool socks, the slim, tapered 3335 may feel tighter in the toes. He hasn't said how that compares to the 875s specifically.
